title: International Solar Alliance, CDRI and Global Initiatives

cards.h: India as a leader of coalitions
cards.b:
India has started several global groups in the last decade. Prelims asks where they are headquartered and when they began. Mains asks whether such soft power gets results.

A table of name, year, aim and HQ is the best way to revise.

The International Solar Alliance (ISA) was launched by India and France at COP21, Paris, on 30 November 2015. Its HQ is at Gurugram, Haryana, hosted on the NIWE campus. The Framework Agreement came into force in December 2017, making ISA a treaty-based international organisation.

It works with the "sunshine countries" between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. A 2020 amendment opened membership to all UN member states. Its aim is to mobilise US$1 trillion by 2030 for solar and to cut costs. The slogan is "One Sun, One World, One Grid".

cards.h: One Sun One World One Grid
cards.b: OSOWOG was announced by PM Modi at the first ISA Assembly (2018) and elaborated at COP26 (2021) as a Green Grids Initiative with the UK. It would link solar-rich areas across regions by cross-border grids, so that the sun is always shining somewhere to feed demand. Phases include India to Gulf and Southeast Asia, then to Africa, then a global grid. Its backers say it cuts costs and storage needs.

CDRI was launched by India at the UN Climate Action Summit, New York, in September 2019. The Secretariat is in New Delhi. It helps countries build roads, power and telecom that survive hazards, and it supports small island developing states. It is a partnership of national governments, UN agencies, multilateral banks and the private sector.

It links to the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030), adopted at the UN conference in Sendai, Japan, in 2015.

• LeadIT (Leadership Group for Industry Transition, 2019): India and Sweden, heavy industry decarbonisation.
  • Global Biofuels Alliance (2023): launched at the G20 in New Delhi, to promote biofuels such as ethanol.
  • International Big Cat Alliance (2023): Mysuru, seven big cats.
  • Mission LiFE (2022): Lifestyle for Environment, launched with the UN Secretary-General.
  • Mangrove Alliance for Climate (COP27, UAE and Indonesia), which India joined.
  • Global Methane Pledge (2021): India did not sign it.

India's solar targets: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030. The National Solar Mission (2010, under NAPCC) started at 20 GW by 2022, later raised to 100 GW and met around 2024-25 (check the latest). The PM-KUSUM scheme (2019) helps farmers with solar pumps. The PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (2024) targets rooftop solar for 1 crore homes. Bhadla (Rajasthan) is among the world's largest solar parks.

Supporters say the alliances lift India's global role and tie finance to Indian ideas. Critics say ISA has raised smaller money than promised, and India's own solar manufacturing depends on Chinese imports. Dependence on imported cells and modules is a vulnerability, and the PLI scheme for solar modules tries to reduce it.

India is among the top three solar markets. Its credibility rests on cheap solar auctions, rooftop growth and a large target. The ISA's headquarters in India and the CDRI secretariat in Delhi give India agenda-setting power in the Global South.

• ISA: 2015 Paris; HQ Gurugram; treaty in force 2017.
  • CDRI: 2019 New York; Secretariat Delhi.
  • LeadIT: 2019; Sweden and India.
  • Global Biofuels Alliance: 2023 G20.
  • IBCA: 2023 Mysuru.
  • Sendai Framework: 2015-30.

Prelims-style: "The International Solar Alliance is headquartered at" (Gurugram). "CDRI was launched at" (UN Climate Action Summit, 2019).

Mains-style: "Examine India's role in building global climate coalitions." Structure: ISA, CDRI, LeadIT, GBA; aims and results; domestic base (solar capacity); criticisms; way forward.
